No pun intended - Christoph Maria Herbst is on top of his game ... he clearly has the mightier than though down to a ... I am not sure what a professor would call it? But he nails it - while you could argue he is pigeon holed (I think that is what it's called when someone seems to be playing a variation of the same person/character) ... he is so good in doing just that ... that you clearly should not mind him doing just that.

The movie is meant to be the vehicle for the female star - but while they seem to be at the opposite side of the spectrum ... and they are quite different (not just background wise) ... they do need each other. I do not think the movie has many surprises for the viewer ... but it is told in a very interesting and well thought of manner ... and it works on exactly the level it tries to connect with the viewer. Tried to watch it in cinemas back then, but was not able to ... caught it on the web (streaming)

This could have been an amazing movie. It is nicely shot, music and scenery well done. It is over all enjoyable, don't get me wrong. But the movie script must read like it was written for the male lead Christoph Maria Herbst. And that is the problem of the movie. The surrounding characters are so cliché drenched and roughly skatched - it makes you wonder if the authors didn't have enough time to finish the script.

I'm sure they cast great actors, but especially Naima's circle of friends show a pretty distorted image of those young adults. The script missed a great story line here and leaves the actors with lines so weak, they end up looking like they are performing sketches about Ghetto kids.

To close on a positive note: I felt like they walked the thin line quite well of using the male lead's degrading language and racial slurs. So if you see it on Netflix or free Tv - enjoy the evening and maybe iron your laundry while watching it. But it isn't really movie theater material from my perspective.

Prepping an offended law student for a debatting compeitition is the "penance" that a professor must undergo for some inopportune words. The movie follows a fairly predictable path of social burden that inhibits ascendancy. But the film deploys a heavy treacle of aestheticism to cover over the cracks. A real missed opportunity to speak to the realities of immigrants in Getmany.

Let's start with the professor. Christoph Maria Herbst fits this role perfectly. That arrogance, that sharp way with words, that constant sense of speaking from a position where he is used to controlling the room it suits him completely. He does not play the character in a flat way and not like some caricature either, but in a way where you immediately understand why he rubs people the wrong way and why he still stays interesting.

Then there is Naima and that is exactly where the film works best for me. Because Nilam Farooq is not just there as a counterweight, but as someone who can really push back against him. Not only in what she says, but in her presence. The two of them have exactly the kind of chemistry a film like this needs. That friction, that measuring each other, that back-and-forth, without it ever feeling forced.

And that is exactly why Contra works.

Because the film does not turn all of this prejudice, background, language, the way people present themselves into just a clean message it wants to deliver. It lets it clash. It lets these characters collide, characters who cannot stand each other at first, and that is exactly where the film finds its strength. One speaks down from above, the other has to prove herself in a space that does not seem built for her and that dynamic is what carries the whole thing.

What I liked is that the film never forgets it still has to entertain. This is not some heavy moral lecture. It knows what its themes are, but still packages them in a way that keeps you engaged. Especially because all that debating is not only happening on a stage, but is constantly going on between the characters themselves.

And maybe that is really the point: Contra works like a debate in which both sides think they have already won and that is exactly why it is interesting to watch the balance slowly shift.

For me, it is a good film with two leads who really carry the whole thing together.

This movie is a german remake (directed by Sonke Wortmann) of the french original Le brio. This remake is well done and shines with the superb acting by Nilam Farooq. The storyline is set up early, much of it through images. Yet the movie is not subtle on a cinematic level alone, the whole story is based around rhetoric on the one hand and racism on the other, prejudices on one side and brilliance of roses that grew from concrete (not giving immigrants the same opportunities) on the other. A must watch and with the unfortunate often low quality of german movie productions this one definitely is a very nice piece. Commendable.
